data.text/markdown:
Part 1b: learning the inverse map

Machine learning and inversion for seismologists

data.text/html:
Physics from Part 1a, unchanged:
def travel_times(m_x, m_y, xi_x, xi_y, v_ref):
    """Forward operator F(m; xi): straight rays at constant P speed.

    m_x, m_y: source coordinates (km), tensors of shape (...)
    xi_x, xi_y: station coordinates (km), shape (N,)
    v_ref: P speed (km/s)
    returns: travel time (s) from every source to every station, shape (..., N)
    """
    delta_x = m_x[..., None] - xi_x
    delta_y = m_y[..., None] - xi_y
    Delta = torch.sqrt(delta_x**2 + delta_y**2)
    return Delta / v_ref


def center(d):
    """Station-mean projection C d = d - <d>: removes the origin time t0.

    d: (..., N) times (s), either picks or travel times
    returns: centred times, shape (..., N), with zero mean over the stations
    """
    return d - d.mean(-1, keepdim=True)


def simulate_picks(m_x, m_y, xi_x, xi_y, v_ref, sigma, t0, generator=None):
    """Noisy P arrival times d_obs = t0 + F(m) + eps with eps ~ N(0, sigma^2).

    m_x, m_y, xi_x, xi_y, v_ref: as in ``travel_times``
    sigma: standard deviation of a pick (s)
    t0: origin time (s), unknown to the inversion
    generator: optional torch.Generator, for reproducible noise
    returns: arrival times (s), shape (..., N)
    """
    F = travel_times(m_x, m_y, xi_x, xi_y, v_ref)
    eps = sigma * torch.randn(F.shape, dtype=F.dtype, generator=generator)
    return t0 + F + eps

data.text/markdown:
What is a multilayer perceptron?

The network that will learn ||(\tilde{\mathbf{d}} \mapsto \mathbf{m}||) is a multilayer perceptron (MLP): a chain of layers, each one a matrix, a bias and a fixed nonlinear function ||(\varphi||), ||[ \mathbf{h}^{(\ell)} = \varphi\!\left(\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}\, \mathbf{h}^{(\ell-1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(\ell)}\right) \qquad \ell = 1, \dots, L ||]started at ||(\mathbf{h}^{(0)} = \tilde{\mathbf{d}}||) and ended by a linear layer, ||(\mathbf{m} = \mathbf{W}^{(L+1)} \mathbf{h}^{(L)} + \mathbf{b}^{(L+1)}||). The entries of ||(\mathbf{W}||) and ||(\mathbf{b}||) are trainable parameters. Training adjusts them through stochastic gradient descent.

data.text/html:
Four things to look for

  • Flexibility. What do width, depth and the activation each add to the curve a network can draw?
  • Initialisation. Does the same network always find the same fit?
  • Held-out points. What do the validation points show that the train loss cannot?
  • Data. How many points before the two losses agree?

data.text/markdown:
How the playground works

One number in, one number out. Draw any curve ||(y(x)||) on the output plot (or pick an example under data) and a network is trained to pass through your points, with the mean squared error as ||(S||). + / − set the depth and the width of each hidden layer; the header sets the activation ||(\varphi||), the step size and the number of epochs, and RETRAIN says whether the network trains again at every change (on change) or only when you press TRAIN (on button). Each tile is one neuron and shows its output ||(h(x)||). ▶ plays the training back from the initial weights, ⏭ steps, ↺ draws new initial weights. Hover an edge, a matrix cell or a neuron to see what it does, click to pin it. The train points (●) are what the network is fitted to. The validation points (○) are never fitted: only their error is computed, after every epoch, and drawn next to the train loss. Choose the set under data before you draw (shift-drag erases). The idea comes from the TensorFlow Playground.

data.text/html:
Setup. Start with one unit and add more, then add a layer; step (⏭) through. Look for. One unit makes one bend. Each neuron of a second layer bends a mix of the layer before, so the pieces multiply.
Setup. Switch between ReLU, tanh and linear. Look for. ReLU: straight pieces. tanh: smooth steps. linear: a straight line, however wide or deep.
Setup. Press ↺ a few times, with ReLU. Look for. New initial weights, a different fit. Some neurons are dead: flat tiles, zero output for every ||(x||), no gradient.
Setup. Load sine, width 16, three layers, 3000 epochs. Look for. The train loss falls far below the noise in the data, the validation loss does not follow: overfitting.
Setup. Choose validation and draw where there are no train points. Look for. The fit is only checked where validation points are.
Setup. Move TRAIN from 6 to 200 points. Look for. With few, the train loss goes to zero while the validation loss stays high; with many, the two come together.
Setup. Set VALIDATION to 3, then to 200. Look for. A few points give a number you cannot trust.

data.text/markdown:
What the curve fit showed

  • Flexibility. Networks can fit complex curves from basic components
  • Overfitting Networks can be too confident.
In the next example the network takes the arrival times at ||(N||) stations and returns 2 values (the epicentre). Data is generated synthetically.

The prior: where we expect events

To fit a neural network the data can either be collected from real events or, if we understand the system sufficiently well, be generated synthetically. Since ground truth locations for earthquakes is hard to come by and seismic wave propagation is well understood, we will generate our dataset here synthetically. But we need to be fully aware that this is always a (big) simplification. Where we expect events before seeing any arrival times is described by the prior distribution ||(\rho_M(\mathbf{m})||).
  • The uniform prior puts events anywhere on the map
  • The ridgecrest prior is inspired by the 2019 Ridgecrest aftershocks

From a source to a training pair

To generate synthetic data, draw a source from the prior, then simulate the noisy centered picks it would produce: ||[ \mathbf{m} \sim \rho_M \qquad \tilde{\mathbf{d}} = \mathbf{C}\,\big(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{m}) + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\big) ||]The data set we use to train the notebook is a long list of pairs ||((\tilde{\mathbf{d}}, \mathbf{m})||). Here we have the luxury that the simulator can make as many as we want.

The simulator in code

observe is the simulator: picks at the stations for a batch of sources, with fresh noise, centred over the working stations (a muted one reads 0). make_dataset draws training and validation events from the training prior, each from its own random stream, so the validation events stay fixed when the number of training events changes. It reads everything from config, the settings the playground's train button captured.

def observe(F, m, sigma, live, generator=None):
    """Centred noisy picks d~ = C (F(m) + eps): what the locator network sees.

    F: forward operator, F(m_x, m_y) -> travel times (s), shape (n, N)
    m: sources (km), shape (n, 2)
    sigma: standard deviation of a pick (s)
    live: which stations work, bool, shape (N,); a muted station is left out of the
        mean and reads 0
    generator: optional torch.Generator, for reproducible noise
    returns: centred picks (s), shape (n, N)
    """
    F_m = F(m[:, 0], m[:, 1])
    d = F_m + sigma * torch.randn(F_m.shape, dtype=F_m.dtype, generator=generator)
    d_c = d - d[:, live].mean(-1, keepdim=True)
    return d_c * live

Train, validation, test

A network that fits its training events does not necessarily generalise to unseen events, to test this datset is split into three sets with different jobs.
  • Train: the network is fitted to these and to nothing else
  • Validation: held back during training, used to adapt training process
  • Test: used once, at the end, for an honest estimate on events the network has never seen

Picks in, location out

The default network is a multilayer perceptron, with one input per station and two outputs, the epicentre: ||[ \hat{\mathbf{m}} = f\big(\tilde{\mathbf{d}}\big) ||]This one has two hidden layers of 16 tanh neurons.

Put numbers on one scale

  • Network weights start at order one, so a network learns best when its inputs and outputs are of order one too.
  • Picks are seconds, locations tens of kilometres. Both are shifted and divided by their standard deviation
||[ \tilde{\mathbf{d}} \mapsto \frac{\tilde{\mathbf{d}}}{\mathrm{std}(\tilde{\mathbf{d}})} \qquad \mathbf{m} \mapsto \frac{\mathbf{m} - \mathrm{mean}(\mathbf{m})}{\mathrm{std}(\mathbf{m})} ||]with the mean and standard deviation of the training events only. Validation and test events must be treated exactly like new data.

What the network is trained on

Gradient descent with unknown weights and biases ||(\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{b}||). The misfit is the mean squared error of the network's answer, in the scaled units, ||[ S = \mathrm{mean}\,\big\Vert \hat{\mathbf{m}} - \mathbf{m} \big\Vert_2^2 ||]and autodiff supplies ||(\nabla S||) for every weight. The optimiser (SGD or Adam) steps against it with step size ||(\eta||), ||[ \mathbf{W} \leftarrow \mathbf{W} - \eta\,\nabla_{\mathbf{W}} S ||]We report the RMS location error in km, which is easier to read than ||(S||).

Epochs and mini-batches

A step after all events would be slow. To avoid this, events are shuffled and cut into mini-batches: one batch, one step. One pass through all events is an epoch, with a new shuffle each time.
  • Small batches: noisy steps that can shake the weights out of a poor local minimum.
  • Larger batches: less noisy gradient, still cheaper (memory and compute) than all at once
  • One batch: the exact gradient, straight into the nearest minimum, expensive per step

    const p = n.parentElement;

    const u = Array.from(n.nodeValue, it).join("");
    if (u !== n.nodeValue) n.nodeValue = u;

  const walk = root => {

<script>
  const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);
  const N = 1000, X0 = 20, W = 1060;
  const OPTIONS = [1, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, N];
  let B = 8;
  const steps = () => Math.ceil(N / B);
  const gap = () => steps() === 1 ? 0 : Math.min(16, 0.45 * W / steps());
  const cell = () => (W - (steps() - 1) * gap()) / N;
  const xOf = k => X0 + k * cell() + Math.floor(k / B) * gap();

  // a fixed shuffle (seeded), so the picture does not change between visits
  const perm = (() => {
    let seed = 7;
    const r = () => { seed = (seed + 0x6D2B79F5) | 0; let t = Math.imul(seed ^ (seed >>> 15), 1 | seed);
      t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t; return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296; };
    const a = Array.from({ length: N }, (_, i) => i);
    for (let i = N - 1; i > 0; i--) { const j = Math.floor(r() * (i + 1)); [a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]]; }
    return a;
  })();

  const shade = i => (0.14 + 0.86 * i / (N - 1)).toFixed(3);
  const rect = (x, y, w, h, i) =>
    `<rect x="${x.toFixed(2)}" y="${y}" width="${w.toFixed(2)}" height="${h}" fill="var(--c1)" fill-opacity="${shade(i)}"/>`;
  const bw = w => Math.max(w - (w > 3 ? 1 : 0), 0.7);

  function draw() {
    let a = "", b = "";
    for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) a += rect(X0 + i * W / N, 72, bw(W / N), 34, i);
    for (let k = 0; k < N; k++) b += rect(xOf(k), 160, bw(cell()), 34, perm[k]);
    $("stripA").innerHTML = a;
    $("stripB").innerHTML = b;
    hover(null);
    document.querySelectorAll("#seg button").forEach(
      e => e.classList.toggle("on", +e.dataset.b === B));
    marks();
  }

  function marks() {
    const n = steps(), y = 204;
    let g = "";
    if (n <= 128)
      for (let b = 0; b < n; b++) {
        const x0 = xOf(b * B), x1 = xOf(Math.min((b + 1) * B, N) - 1) + cell();
        g += `<path class="br" d="M${x0.toFixed(1)} ${y - 4}V${y}H${x1.toFixed(1)}V${y - 4}"/>`;
        if (n <= 16) g += `<text class="dim" x="${((x0 + x1) / 2).toFixed(1)}" y="${y + 14}" ` +
          `text-anchor="middle">step ${b + 1}</text>`;
      }
    const ye = n <= 16 ? 236 : 222;
    g += `<path class="brE" d="M${X0} ${ye - 5}V${ye}H${X0 + W}V${ye - 5}"/>` +
      `<text x="${X0 + W / 2}" y="${ye + 17}" text-anchor="middle">one epoch: ` +
      `all ${N} events seen once, in ${n} ${n === 1 ? "step" : "steps"}</text>`;
    $("marks").innerHTML = g;
  }

  function hover(b) {
    const cur = $("cur");
    if (b === null) { cur.style.display = "none"; $("hov").textContent = ""; return; }
    const first = b * B, size = Math.min(B, N - first);
    cur.style.display = "";
    cur.setAttribute("x", (xOf(first) - 2.5).toFixed(2));
    cur.setAttribute("y", 156);
    cur.setAttribute("width", (size * cell() + 5).toFixed(2));
    cur.setAttribute("height", 42);
    $("hov").textContent = `step ${b + 1} of ${steps()}: ${size} events, one update of the weights`;
  }

  const svg = $("strips");
  $("hit").addEventListener("pointermove", ev => {
    const p = new DOMPoint(ev.clientX, ev.clientY).matrixTransform(svg.getScreenCTM().inverse());
    const b = Math.floor((p.x - X0) / (B * cell() + gap()));
    hover(Math.min(Math.max(b, 0), steps() - 1));
  });
  $("hit").addEventListener("pointerleave", () => hover(null));

  $("seg").innerHTML = OPTIONS.map(o =>
    `<button data-b="${o}">${o === N ? "all" : o}</button>`).join("");
  $("seg").onclick = ev => {
    const b = ev.target.closest("button");
    if (b) { B = +b.dataset.b; draw(); }
  };
  draw();
</script>
</body>
</html>

data.text/markdown:
The best possible locator

  • The data say how likely each location is: the likelihood.
  • Combined with the prior, it gives the posterior: the full probabilistic answer for one event.
  • Under a squared error the best single answer is the posterior mean, no network can beat this
  • The floor is not zero, because the picks are noisy.
The figure uses noisier picks than usual, so that the prior can be seen.

Reading learning curves

There are generally thre kind of behaviours you can see in learning curves:
  • Underfit: both errors stay high, well above the floor. The network is too simple.
  • A good fit: both errors fall and level off a little above the floor.
  • Overfit: the training error keeps falling while the validation error turns up.

A network knows only its simulator

Training and validation error come from the same simulator, so neither can show that the simulator is wrong. The real world can differ in three ways:
  • The prior: events where the training prior put none.
  • The physics: a P-speed model other than the one that made the training picks.
  • The stations: one moved or had a failure, so the same input now means something else.

How the playground works

Work from the top down.
  • Scene. Stations (+ / −; drag to move, double-click empty ground to add one, shift-click to mute a dead one), P-speed model and pick noise ||(\sigma||).
  • Data. Number of training events, training and test prior.
  • Network. Hidden layers, one width per layer, activation.
  • Training. Optimiser, step size ||(\eta||), batch size, epochs and rescale.
The network retrains as soon as you change a setting, in well under a second, and the run plays back (▶ pauses, ⏭ steps, the bar scrubs). Set RETRAIN to on button to keep a trained network and change only the data, then press TRAIN for a new one. Runs that would take more than a few seconds always wait for the button. Two maps share the scene; each shows a background of your choice: the P speed (with the rays from the test event), the prior (with the training events), the error of the network for a source anywhere (arrows show where its answers are pulled), or the posterior or likelihood of the test event (68 % and 95 % regions, ◆ its mean). Drag the test event (star): the orange dot is the network's answer, the small dots are its answers for 64 noise draws of the same event. The network you chose is drawn under the playground: the learned weights, or the initial weights (grey) while a retraining is pending. With on button, moving or muting a station or switching the P speed changes the data but not the network. The posterior keeps the P speed and ||(\sigma||) of the training (dashed rays), while the data follow the new scene (solid).
